---
marp: true
paginate: true
style: |
  /*
   * Percona Live 2026 Amsterdam. Lives here, in the front matter, so every Marp renderer
   * picks it up with no configuration — VS Code preview, marp CLI, marp.app.
   *
   * The backgrounds in assets/ are the template PDF's own pages, so the artwork is the
   * template's rather than a re-drawing of it. Palette and safe zones are measured off it:
   * charcoal #282727, white, violet #653DF4, lime #F6FE54.
   *
   * Classes:  (none) light content  |  dark  |  title  |  section  |  dense
   */


  :root {
    --charcoal: #282727;
    --white: #ffffff;
    --violet: #653df4;
    --lime: #f6fe54;
  }

  section {
    width: 1280px;
    height: 720px;
    font-family: 'Poppins', 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif;
    font-weight: 300;
    font-size: 22px;
    line-height: 1.42;
    letter-spacing: 0;
    color: var(--charcoal);
    background: var(--white) var(--bg-light) center / cover no-repeat;
    /* the light master's charcoal wedge eats the bottom-left corner */
    padding: 96px 100px 150px 166px;
  }

  section.dark {
    color: var(--white);
    background-image: var(--bg-dark);
    /* its corner mark is much smaller, so the column can start further left */
    padding: 96px 230px 120px 102px;
  }

  section.title {
    color: var(--white);
    background-image: var(--bg-title);
    /* the lockup owns the left third; the photo cuts in from the right */
    padding: 108px 358px 0 448px;
  }

  section.section {
    color: var(--white);
    background-image: var(--bg-dark);
    padding: 0 230px 0 102px;
    display: flex;
    flex-direction: column;
    place-content: center;         /* dividers keep the vertical centring */
  }

  /* --- type ---------------------------------------------------------------- */

  h1 {
    font-weight: 600;
    font-size: 48px;
    line-height: 1.14;
    letter-spacing: -0.01em;
    margin: 0 0 18px;
  }

  h2 {
    font-weight: 600;
    font-size: 35px;
    line-height: 1.15;
    letter-spacing: -0.01em;
    margin: 0 0 28px;
  }

  section.title h1 {
    font-size: 44px;
    line-height: 1.14;
    letter-spacing: -0.01em;
  }

  /* the speaker lines on the title slide sit under the lockup, not in the title column */
  section.title p {
    position: absolute;
    left: 102px;
    width: 42%;
    margin: 0;
    font-size: 18px;
    line-height: 1.6;
    opacity: .92;
  }

  section.title p:nth-of-type(1) { top: 590px; }
  section.title p:nth-of-type(2) { top: 619px; }

  ul {
    margin: 0;
    padding: 0;
    list-style: none;
  }

  li {
    margin: 0 0 16px;
    padding-left: 28px;
    position: relative;
  }

  li::before {
    content: '';
    position: absolute;
    left: 0;
    top: .58em;
    width: 10px;
    height: 10px;
    background: var(--violet);
    clip-path: polygon(0 0, 100% 50%, 0 100%);
  }

  section.dark li::before { background: var(--lime); }

  li > ul { margin-top: 10px; }
  li > ul > li { font-size: .9em; opacity: .85; }

  strong { font-weight: 600; }
  em { font-style: italic; }

  code {
    font-family: 'SF Mono', ui-monospace, Menlo, monospace;
    font-size: .86em;
    background: rgba(101, 61, 244, .12);
    border-radius: 4px;
    padding: 1px 6px;
  }

  section.dark code,
  section.title code { background: rgba(255, 255, 255, .14); }

  pre {
    font-size: 18px;
    border-left: 4px solid var(--violet);
    padding-left: 18px;
  }

  /* --- the takeaway line: write it as a blockquote -------------------------- */

  blockquote {
    margin: 22px 0 0;
    padding: 2px 0 2px 18px;
    border-left: 5px solid var(--violet);
    font-weight: 600;
    font-size: 23px;
    line-height: 1.3;
  }

  section.dark blockquote { border-left-color: var(--lime); }
  blockquote p { margin: 0; }

  /* --- tables --------------------------------------------------------------- */

  table {
    font-size: 19px;
    border-collapse: collapse;
    width: 100%;
  }

  th {
    font-weight: 600;
    text-align: left;
    border-bottom: 2px solid var(--violet);
    padding: 8px 12px 8px 0;
  }

  td {
    font-weight: 300;
    border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(40, 39, 39, .12);
    padding: 8px 12px 8px 0;
  }

  section.dark td { border-bottom-color: rgba(255, 255, 255, .16); }

  /* --- long slides tighten up rather than run into the wedge ---------------- */

  section.dense h2,
  section:has(li:nth-child(6)) h2 { font-size: 30px; margin-bottom: 22px; }

  section.dense li,
  section:has(li:nth-child(6)) li { font-size: 19px; margin-bottom: 12px; }

  section.dense blockquote,
  section:has(li:nth-child(6)) blockquote { font-size: 20px; margin-top: 18px; }

  /* --- override Marp's default theme ---------------------------------------
   * An inline style block is layered on top of the built-in theme rather than
   * replacing it, so its per-element colours and blockquote quote marks have to
   * be undone explicitly. Everything below just says "inherit from the slide".
   */

  section h1, section h2, section h3, section h4, section h5, section h6,
  section p, section ul, section ol, section li, section blockquote,
  section table, section th, section td, section strong, section em, section code {
    color: inherit;
  }

  section {
    color: var(--charcoal);
    /* the built-in theme centres content with `place-content: safe center center`,
       and place-content is the only thing that overrides it */
    display: block;
    place-content: start;
  }

  section.dark,
  section.title,
  section.section { color: var(--white); }

  section blockquote::before,
  section blockquote::after { content: none; }

  section a { color: var(--violet); }
  section.dark a, section.title a { color: var(--lime); }

  /* --- pagination ----------------------------------------------------------- */

  section::after {
    font-family: 'Poppins', sans-serif;
    font-weight: 300;
    font-size: 14px;
    color: var(--charcoal);
    opacity: .45;
    padding: 0;            /* Marp pads it by the section padding otherwise */
    right: 58px;
    bottom: 40px;
  }

  /* the dark master parks its logo bottom-right, so the number goes left */
  section.dark::after {
    color: var(--white);
    right: auto;
    left: 102px;
  }

  /* --- diagram + emphasis toolkit ------------------------------------------
   * Diagrams are inline SVG, which Marp passes through untouched — no config,
   * no flags, no external files, consistent with the rest of this deck.
   *
   * They never hard-code a colour. Every SVG paints with --ink / --accent /
   * --panel / --edge / --dim, which are re-pointed per master below, so the
   * same markup reads correctly on the light slide and on the charcoal one.
   *
   *   <figure><svg class="d" viewBox="0 0 1014 300">…</svg></figure>
   *
   * Widths to author against (the masters' safe zones):
   *   light slide  1014 x ~300     dark slide  948 x ~330
   *   .aside slide   470 wide figure, text takes the rest
   */

  section {
    --ink: var(--charcoal);
    --accent: var(--violet);
    --panel: rgba(101, 61, 244, .07);
    --edge: rgba(40, 39, 39, .22);
    --dim: rgba(40, 39, 39, .5);
  }

  section.dark,
  section.section,
  section.title {
    --ink: var(--white);
    --accent: var(--lime);
    --panel: rgba(255, 255, 255, .06);
    --edge: rgba(255, 255, 255, .24);
    --dim: rgba(255, 255, 255, .55);
  }

  figure { margin: 18px 0 0; }

  svg.d { display: block; width: 100%; height: auto; overflow: visible; }

  svg.d text {
    font-family: 'Poppins', 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif;
    font-weight: 300;
    font-size: 17px;
    fill: var(--ink);
  }

  svg.d .b    { font-weight: 600; }
  svg.d .sm   { font-size: 14px; fill: var(--dim); }
  svg.d .xs   { font-size: 12px; fill: var(--dim); letter-spacing: .04em; }
  svg.d .mono { font-family: 'SF Mono', ui-monospace, Menlo, monospace; font-size: 14px; }

  svg.d .box  { fill: var(--panel); stroke: var(--edge); stroke-width: 1.5; }
  svg.d .box-a{ fill: var(--panel); stroke: var(--accent); stroke-width: 2.5; }
  svg.d .ln   { stroke: var(--edge); stroke-width: 1.5; fill: none; }
  svg.d .ln-a { stroke: var(--accent); stroke-width: 2.5; fill: none; }
  svg.d .dash { stroke: var(--edge); stroke-width: 1.5; fill: none; stroke-dasharray: 5 5; }
  svg.d .acc  { fill: var(--accent); }
  svg.d .ghost{ fill: var(--panel); }

  /* --- a diagram beside the text, rather than under it ---------------------- */

  section.aside { padding-right: 560px; }
  section.aside figure {
    position: absolute;
    right: 78px;
    top: 168px;
    width: 462px;
    margin: 0;
  }
  section.aside.dark { padding-right: 560px; }

  /* a narrower column wraps more, so .aside tightens like .dense does */
  section.aside h2 { font-size: 30px; margin-bottom: 20px; }
  section.aside li { font-size: 19px; margin-bottom: 12px; }
  section.aside blockquote { font-size: 20px; margin-top: 16px; }

  /* --- the one-line slide: no bullets, just the statement ------------------- */

  section.hero h2 {
    font-size: 60px;
    line-height: 1.06;
    letter-spacing: -0.02em;
    max-width: 15ch;
  }
  section.hero blockquote { margin-top: 32px; font-size: 26px; }

  /* --- an imported diagram, given almost the whole slide -------------------- */

  /* Left and top match section.dark exactly, so the heading sits in the same
     column as every other slide. Right and bottom are pulled in only as far as
     the master's own artwork needs: the photo cuts in top-right, the lockup
     sits bottom-right. */
  section.full { padding: 96px 190px 104px 102px; }
  section.full img { display: block; width: 100%; height: auto; border-radius: 10px; }
  section.full img + .footnote { margin: 18px 0 0; }

  /* --- a quiet line under the content, for scope caveats -------------------- */

  .footnote {
    margin: -14px 0 20px;
    font-size: 16px;
    line-height: 1.4;
    color: var(--dim);
  }

  /* --- a label above the heading -------------------------------------------- */

  .kicker {
    font-size: 13px;
    font-weight: 600;
    letter-spacing: .16em;
    text-transform: uppercase;
    color: var(--accent);
    margin: 0 0 12px;
  }

  /* --- a row of terms, for slides that are really just a vocabulary --------- */

  .chips { margin: 4px 0 0; padding: 0; }
  .chips span {
    display: inline-block;
    margin: 0 8px 10px 0;
    padding: 6px 14px;
    border: 1.5px solid var(--edge);
    border-radius: 999px;
    font-size: 17px;
  }
  .chips span.on {
    border-color: var(--accent);
    background: var(--panel);
    font-weight: 600;
  }

  /* --- the four numbers, and slides shaped like them ------------------------ */

  .stats { display: flex; gap: 42px; margin: 26px 0 0; }
  .stats div { flex: 1; }
  .stats b {
    display: block;
    min-height: 2.2em;   /* a two-line figure must not drop its label out of line */
    font-size: 40px;
    font-weight: 600;
    letter-spacing: -0.02em;
    line-height: 1.1;
    color: var(--accent);
  }
  .stats span { display: block; margin-top: 6px; font-size: 17px; }

  /* --- section dividers get the running order ------------------------------- */

  section.section h1 { font-size: 58px; max-width: 16ch; }
  section.section .kicker { margin-bottom: 18px; }

  /* --- inlined assets: generated, don't hand-edit (see README) ------------
   * The template's own three master pages and the Poppins subsets, inlined so the
   * deck renders identically in the VS Code preview, marp.app and the CLI, with no
   * local-file access and no configuration.
   */
  :root {
    --bg-light: url(data:image/jpeg;base64,);
    --bg-dark: url(data:image/jpeg;base64,);
    --bg-title: url(data:image/jpeg;base64,);
  }
  @font-face { font-family: 'Poppins'; font-style: normal; font-weight: 300; font-display: block; src: url(data:font/woff2;base64,) format('woff2'); }
  @font-face { font-family: 'Poppins'; font-style: normal; font-weight: 600; font-display: block; src: url(data:font/woff2;base64,) format('woff2'); }

Percona Live 2026 Amsterdam

George Kechagias, Senior Software Engineer, Percona

# The layer under the layer 🧱

<!--
0:00–0:05, 5 min
-->

---

## Everything the operator layer gives you

- **Control loops**: failover, backup and scaling run as code, continuously
- **A CR per cluster**: one declarative, versioned API object, validated by the API server
- **The platform's own objects**: RBAC, Secrets, StorageClasses, and the wider ecosystem
- **Portable by construction**: GKE, EKS, AKS, OpenShift, bare metal — same CR, local classes
- **A fleet you can review**: every database in the estate is a file in a git repository

```yaml
apiVersion: ps.percona.com/v1
```

## The whole storage provisioning API is a couple of lines

```yaml
volumeSpec:
  persistentVolumeClaim:
    # storageClassName: db-storage           
    # volumeAttributesClassName: high-perf
    resources: { requests: { storage: 100Gi } }
```

- It's a plain `PersistentVolumeClaimSpec`, nothing operator-shaped about it, to build the PVCs.

<figure>
<svg class="d" viewBox="0 0 1014 126" role="img" aria-label="The three volume sources the operator accepts, and how long data survives on each">
  <text class="xs" x="0" y="14">THE OPERATOR ACCEPTS THREE · IT PICKS THE FIRST ONE YOU SET, IN THIS ORDER</text>
  <rect class="box-a" x="0" y="26" width="324" height="94" rx="10"/>
  <text class="mono b" x="22" y="56" dominant-baseline="middle">persistentVolumeClaim</text>
  <text class="sm" x="22" y="84" dominant-baseline="middle">a real disk, managed by Kubernetes</text>
  <text class="xs" x="22" y="108">survives reschedule to another node</text>
  <rect class="box" x="345" y="26" width="324" height="94" rx="10" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
  <text class="mono b" x="367" y="56" dominant-baseline="middle">hostPath</text>
  <text class="sm" x="367" y="84" dominant-baseline="middle">a directory on that node, as-is</text>
  <text class="xs" x="367" y="108">survives the pod, never leaves the node</text>
  <rect class="box" x="690" y="26" width="324" height="94" rx="10" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
  <text class="mono b" x="712" y="56" dominant-baseline="middle">emptyDir</text>
  <text class="sm" x="712" y="84" dominant-baseline="middle">scratch space, created empty</text>
  <text class="xs" x="712" y="108">deleted with the pod. all of it.</text>
</svg>
</figure>

The precedence is a literal switch in `pkg/mysql/mysql.go`: if `persistentVolumeClaim` is set

why every PVC on my cluster reads `VOLUMEATTRIBUTESCLASS: <unset>`.

If someone asks why emptyDir exists at all: CI, demos, and throwaway clusters. An emptyDir

<!-- _class: aside -->

## Some PVC fields cannot change that easily

- `storageClassName`: fixed for the life of the claim
- `accessModes`: a promise the driver keeps or quietly ignores
- `kubectl delete pvc` takes the disk with it, the class's `reclaimPolicy` decides

<figure>
<svg class="d" viewBox="0 0 462 300" role="img" aria-label="Three fields are set at provisioning time; changing them later is a migration">
  <text class="xs" x="0" y="12">AT PROVISIONING</text>
  <rect class="box-a" x="0" y="26" width="462" height="150" rx="12"/>
  <text class="xs" x="24" y="56">IN YOUR CR, SET ONCE</text>
  <text class="mono b" x="24" y="86" dominant-baseline="middle">storageClassName</text>
  <text class="mono b" x="24" y="122" dominant-baseline="middle">accessModes</text>
  <text class="xs" x="24" y="158">reclaimPolicy lives on the StorageClass, not here</text>
  <path class="ln-a" d="M231 176 V214"/><path class="acc" d="M225 214 l6 12 6 -12 z"/>
  <text class="xs" x="0" y="252">AFTER PROVISIONING</text>
  <rect class="box" x="0" y="262" width="462" height="38" rx="12" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
  <text class="sm" x="24" y="281" dominant-baseline="middle">changing any of them = a migration, not an edit</text>
</svg>
</figure>

## Four ways storage gets to your pod

<figure>
<svg class="d" viewBox="0 0 1014 312" role="img" aria-label="Storage reaches a node four ways: local, as a block device over a network, as a filesystem over a network, or as an HTTP API that is never mounted">
  <text class="xs" x="0" y="14">WHAT THE NODE IS HANDED</text>
  <text class="xs" x="330" y="14">WHAT IT IS</text>
  <text class="xs" x="640" y="14">WHO OWNS THE FILESYSTEM</text>
  <rect class="box" x="0" y="26" width="1014" height="62" rx="10"/>
  <text class="b" x="22" y="58" dominant-baseline="middle">a disk on the node</text>
  <text class="mono" x="330" y="58" dominant-baseline="middle" style="font-size:14px">local NVMe · LocalPV · hostPath</text>
  <text class="sm" x="640" y="58" dominant-baseline="middle">your kernel. dies with the node.</text>
  <rect class="box-a" x="0" y="100" width="1014" height="62" rx="10"/>
  <text class="b" x="22" y="132" dominant-baseline="middle">a block device, remote</text>
  <text class="mono" x="330" y="132" dominant-baseline="middle" style="font-size:14px">EBS · PD · Ceph RBD · iSCSI</text>
  <text class="sm" x="640" y="132" dominant-baseline="middle">your kernel formats it. RWO.</text>
  <rect class="box" x="0" y="174" width="1014" height="62" rx="10"/>
  <text class="b" x="22" y="206" dominant-baseline="middle">a filesystem, remote</text>
  <text class="mono" x="330" y="206" dominant-baseline="middle" style="font-size:14px">EFS · Filestore · NFS · CephFS</text>
  <text class="sm" x="640" y="206" dominant-baseline="middle">their server owns it. RWX.</text>
  <rect class="box" x="0" y="248" width="1014" height="62" rx="10"/>
  <text class="b" x="22" y="280" dominant-baseline="middle">an HTTP API, never mounted</text>
  <text class="mono" x="330" y="280" dominant-baseline="middle" style="font-size:14px">S3 · GCS · Azure Blob</text>
  <text class="sm" x="640" y="280" dominant-baseline="middle">nobody. it is not a filesystem.</text>
</svg>
</figure>

Land it: A block device is not a local disk. It just looks like one from inside the container.

Worth saying once, because it is the hidden subject of the slide: the pod attaches nothing.
The NODE is handed the storage, and the kubelet then mounts it into the container. That is
why RWO is enforced per node and not per pod, and why two pods on one node can both mount
the same RWO volume.

The distinction between rows two and three is the whole slide, so say it plainly:

  block = you are handed a disk, and YOUR kernel makes a filesystem on it
  file  = you are handed somebody else's filesystem, already made

That is where RWO and RWX come from. Two kernels cannot both own one ext4 without corrupting
it, so a block device goes to one node at a time. A file server arbitrates between its
clients, so it can serve many.

It is also why databases want row two: they assume local filesystem semantics, fsync that
actually reaches the disk, byte-range locking, no surprise attribute caching. NFS is
historically where those assumptions go to die.

Row two is the one to slow down on, because it is where almost every database in this room
actually lives, and because it is invisible: the kernel sees a block device, the filesystem
sees a block device, and the database has no idea there is a network under it. That hop is
one of the seven layers in act five.

Row three is the tempting wrong answer — RWX solves a problem databases do not have, and
adds a protocol round trip to every operation.

Row four is here so nobody proposes an S3 datadir. Object storage is not mountable in any
way a database can use; it is where backups go.

Sizes matter as much as shapes: the same driver gives you a 2 GiB volume and a 20 TiB one
with wildly different performance, which is the next-but-one slide.

## The Kubernetes object you probably didn't write

```console
kubectl get storageclass              # what your cluster already has
kubectl apply -f db-storage.yaml      # and nothing stops you adding your own
```

```yaml
metadata: { name: db-storage }          # kind: StorageClass · storage.k8s.io/v1
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com            # which driver, and therefore which world
parameters: { type: gp3, iops: "6000", throughput: "250" }
allowVolumeExpansion: true              # or your disk never grows
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer # or it is created in the wrong zone
reclaimPolicy: Delete                   # or kubectl delete pvc takes the disk
```

- Managed clusters ship some already: e.g. `gp2` (EKS), `standard-rwo` (GKE), `default` (AKS)
- `volumeSpec.persistentVolumeClaim.storageClassName: db-storage`

## The provisioner is a driver, and the driver picks the features

- `provisioner:` names the CSI driver that creates the disk — a program, not a K8s feature
- Kubernetes never calls the cloud provider: it calls the driver, the driver calls its API
- Not installed? every claim against that class sits Pending, see: `kubectl get csidrivers`

<figure>
<svg class="d" viewBox="0 0 1014 186" role="img" aria-label="Example CSI provisioners you will meet in the wild, block and file alike">

  <rect class="box-a" x="0" y="26" width="1014" height="160" rx="10"/>
  <text class="mono" x="40" y="68" dominant-baseline="middle">ebs.csi.aws.com</text>
  <text class="mono" x="370" y="68" dominant-baseline="middle">pd.csi.storage.gke.io</text>
  <text class="mono" x="700" y="68" dominant-baseline="middle">rook-ceph.rbd.csi.ceph.com</text>
  <text class="mono" x="40" y="108" dominant-baseline="middle">nfs.csi.k8s.io</text>
  <text class="mono" x="370" y="108" dominant-baseline="middle">disk.csi.azure.com</text>
  <text class="mono" x="700" y="108" dominant-baseline="middle">kubernetes.io/no-provisioner</text>
  <text class="sm" x="40" y="152" dominant-baseline="middle">the class name is chosen by a human. this line is a fact about what your cluster can do.</text>
</svg>
</figure>

Read the six out loud in one pass and say what each one implies, without putting it on the
slide: the first four are block — your kernel formats it, one node holds it, one volume per
replica, which is where a database belongs. `nfs.csi.k8s.io` is file — their server owns the
filesystem, many pods mount it at once. `kubernetes.io/no-provisioner` is local disk: no
driver provisions anything, you pre-create the PV, and the node is the failure domain —
fast, and yours to back up, because there is no snapshot and no reattach.

Why RWX is the tempting wrong answer, if someone asks: people reach for it because "shared
storage" sounds safer. A replicated database does not want one shared filesystem, it wants
one private volume per replica and does its own replication on top. RWX solves "many pods
need the same files", which is a web-assets problem, not a database problem.

Vocabulary callback to "Four ways storage gets to your pod" — block and file are already

## The newest storage object: change IOPS, not size

```console
kubectl get volumeattributesclass     # GA in 1.34, locked in 1.36
```

```yaml
kind: VolumeAttributesClass
metadata: { name: silver }              # another label you point a claim at
driverName: pd.csi.storage.gke.io       # the same driver that provisioned the disk
parameters: { iops: "3000", throughput: "150" }        # driver-specific names
```

- Point a live claim at it and the disk is modified in place — no resize, no new volume
- The parameters are immutable: repoint the claim at another class, don't edit this one

<!--
Land it: Kubernetes finally separated "how fast" from "how big" — as an API, at least

Show it straight after the StorageClass, because it is the same shape on purpose: a name, a

gets created and is frozen into the claim; a VolumeAttributesClass is meant to be swapped on
a claim that already exists, which makes it the only mutable field on a PVC.

The mechanism: set `spec.volumeAttributesClassName` on a bound PVC, and the external-resizer
calls `ControllerModifyVolume` on the driver. Watch `status.modifyVolumeStatus` on the claim
to see whether it took, is pending, or came back Infeasible.

 - Versions: first available in v1.29, generally available in v1.34, and stable/locked since
   v1.36 — the feature gate is ignored from there on. Say "GA since 1.34", not "new in 1.35".
 - Immutability cuts the other way from a StorageClass. The class NAME on a PVC is mutable —
   that is the whole feature — but the PARAMETERS inside an existing class are not. Want
   different numbers? Create another class and repoint the claim. So "silver" and "gold" as
   names in the docs are not a style choice; tiers are how you are meant to use this.

differently. Do not read them as a portable API — the only portable part is the shape.

 - `ControllerModifyVolume` is one more optional CSI capability. The driver only offers it
   where the hardware has something to tune — on GKE that means Hyperdisk, not pd-balanced

it needs `allowVolumeExpansion` on the class and `ControllerExpandVolume` in the driver, so

Land it: The operator's entire storage job is to copy a name into a template and then wait

Worth walking slowly, because most people assume the operator provisions storage. It doesn't.
Reconcile order is Secrets, then Services, then the StatefulSet — and the StatefulSet is where
storage enters. `pkg/mysql/mysql.go` turns `spec.mysql.volumeSpec` into a single
volumeClaimTemplate called `datadir`; `pkg/k8s/pvc.go` is the copy, and it copies exactly
three fields: StorageClassName, AccessModes, Resources.

From there it is the StatefulSet controller, not the operator, that creates
`datadir-<cluster>-mysql-<ordinal>`. That naming is the reason a deleted pod comes back to its
own data: the ordinal is the identity, and the claim is keyed by it. Delete mysql-1, and
mysql-1 reattaches to datadir-cluster1-mysql-1. Delete the claim too, and mysql-1 comes back
empty — and then the slide after next, GTID comparison, decides whether that costs you a full
clone.

The two boxes underneath are the part people get wrong, and both are checked in the source.

Ownership: `EnsureObjectWithHash` in `pkg/k8s/utils.go` sets a controller reference on
everything the operator creates, so the StatefulSet, the Services and the Secrets are garbage
collected with the CR. The PVCs are not created by the operator at all — the StatefulSet
controller makes them, and nothing sets `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` anywhere in
the repo, so the default Retain/Retain applies. Delete the cluster and your claims are still
sitting there. Deleting them is opt-in: `percona.com/delete-mysql-pvc`, which ships COMMENTED
OUT in `deploy/cr.yaml`. Say that out loud — most people assume the opposite, in one
direction or the other, and both mistakes are expensive.

Then it comes back only to grow them: `pkg/controller/ps/volumes.go`, and only when
`storageScaling.enableVolumeScaling` is set. That is the "Growing the volume" slide, two
slides from here. No formatting, no mounting, no snapshots, no CSI calls, ever.

One line worth saying while the third box is up, because it has no slide of its own: nothing
validates the class name. Not the operator, not admission. Get it wrong and there is no error
anywhere — just a PVC that stays Pending with `storageclass.storage.k8s.io "db-storage" not
found` in its events, and a pod that never starts. A typo in your CR surfaces three layers
down as a scheduling problem.
-->

  <path class="ln-a" d="M524 118 H556 V206 H588"/><path class="acc" d="M588 200 l12 6 -12 6 z"/>
  <rect class="box-a" x="612" y="6" width="402" height="94" rx="10"/>
  <text class="b" x="632" y="34" dominant-baseline="middle">CLONE <tspan class="sm">· physical file copy</tspan></text>
  <text class="sm" x="632" y="60" dominant-baseline="middle">diverged, or the binlogs it needs are gone</text>

  <text class="sm" x="632" y="218" dominant-baseline="middle">the primary still has every transaction it missed</text>
  <text class="xs" x="632" y="244">replays transactions</text>

<!--
Land it: The operator decides whether your new replica costs you a full dataset or a few transactions

This is a real decision in the operator's code, not a Kubernetes one:
`cmd/bootstrap/gr/recovery_method.go`, wired in as the StartupProbe at `pkg/mysql/mysql.go`.
It reads GTID_EXECUTED from both members and switches on the relation between the two sets.

 - diverged or irrecoverable        -> clone, always
 - recoverable, identical, or new   -> clone only if the replica is behind the primary by
                                       more than @@GLOBAL.group_replication_clone_threshold
                                       (read from the REPLICA), otherwise incremental

Two things to be accurate about if anyone digs, both checked in the source:

The trigger is not "empty datadir". `group_replication.go` asks mysqlsh for the cluster
topology and only runs this when the local host is absent from it — a new pod, or one coming
back after its claim was deleted, or one that sat out long enough to be dropped. mysqld is
already running locally at that point, which is how both sides can answer SELECT @@GTID_EXECUTED.

The threshold branch almost never fires. The operator never sets
group_replication_clone_threshold, so it is MySQL's default, which is effectively infinite. In
practice clone gets chosen because the sets diverged, or because the replica is new AND the
primary has already purged the binlogs it would need — checked with
GTID_SUBTRACT(purged, replica_executed) = ''. That purged case is the real "empty volume, full
copy" path, not the size of the gap.

The storage consequence is the whole point. A clone is a physical copy of the datadir, so a
1 TB database means 1 TB written to a brand-new empty volume, at whatever your network and
your disk will do. Incremental writes kilobytes. Same CR, same StorageClass, two wildly
different afternoons.

And notice what is NOT involved: no snapshot, no volume clone, no CSI call. The storage layer
just sees an empty volume filling up.

Land it: The one object that outlives the pod is also where the operator writes its mind

Why on the volume and not in the CR? Because the answer has to survive the pod that learned
it. A member that saw a full cluster crash has to still know that after it restarts, and CR
status is written by the operator, not by the dying pod.

Be precise about the second row, because the three behave differently and someone will ask:

 - `full-cluster-crash` does NOT stop MySQL. `ps-entrypoint.sh` prints a banner, calls
   ensure_read_only, and the pod comes up read-only. The file is not empty either: the
   bootstrap writes this node's GTID_EXECUTED into it, which is exactly what you need to
   pick a reboot candidate.
 - `sleep-forever` is the one that really does not start. The entrypoint enters an infinite
   loop before mysqld, and stays there until a human deletes the file.
 - `clusterset-recovery` is the operator telling the pod to forget: when it exists, the
   bootstrap deletes no-bootstrap, sleep-forever and full-cluster-crash, then removes it.

`pkg/controller/ps/crash_recovery.go` is a whole reconciler built on one of these: it looks
for `/var/lib/mysql/full-cluster-crash` on every member, and if `spec.mysql.autoRecovery` is
off it refuses to act and tells you to run `dba.rebootClusterFromCompleteOutage()` yourself.

Also worth knowing, if asked who writes them: the top row is the container entrypoint, not
the controller. `bootstrap.lock` is touched around datadir init and around the grant re-apply
that a CR version bump triggers; `clone.lock` is written AFTER a successful clone so the next
restart does not clone again; `cr-version` is stamped at the very end of the entrypoint and is
how it notices an upgrade next time.

This is the "I did not know that" slide of the first half, because it breaks an assumption:
people debug a stuck cluster by looking at pods and events, and the actual answer is a file
inside the datadir.
-->

## Growing the volume, without the downtime

<figure>
<svg class="d" viewBox="0 0 1014 116" role="img" aria-label="The resize sequence: edit each PVC, wait for the driver, then recreate the StatefulSet with cascade orphan">
  <rect class="box-a" x="0" y="30" width="228" height="72" rx="10"/>
  <text class="b" x="20" y="56" dominant-baseline="middle">1 · edit each PVC</text>
  <text class="xs" x="20" y="80" dominant-baseline="middle">in place, one per ordinal</text>
  <path class="ln-a" d="M228 66 H266"/><path class="acc" d="M266 60 l12 6 -12 6 z"/>
  <rect class="box-a" x="290" y="30" width="228" height="72" rx="10"/>
  <text class="b" x="310" y="56" dominant-baseline="middle">2 · watch conditions</text>
  <text class="xs" x="310" y="80" dominant-baseline="middle">until every claim reports it</text>
  <path class="ln-a" d="M518 66 H556"/><path class="acc" d="M556 60 l12 6 -12 6 z"/>
  <rect class="box-a" x="580" y="30" width="228" height="72" rx="10"/>

```yaml
  autoscaling:
    enabled: true
    triggerThresholdPercent: 80   # default; clamped to 50–95
    growthStep: 2Gi               # default
    maxSize: 100Gi                # optional ceiling
```

# What Kubernetes does underneath ⚙️

<!--
0:18–0:28, 10 min
-->

---

## Why your storage driver is not part of Kubernetes

- **Container Storage Interface**: one gRPC API for block and file storage, any orchestrator
- Before it, drivers lived **in-tree**: fixes waited for a Kubernetes release · GA in 1.13
- Vendors write the drivers (AWS, Google, Ceph) and ship them as pods in your cluster
- Most CSI calls are optional: your feature set is whatever that driver advertises
- Kubernetes' half is sidecar containers: `external-provisioner`, `external-attacher`, `external-resizer`, making the CSI calls that the driver answers


<!--
Land it: Kubernetes got out of the storage business, and handed your feature set to a vendor

Sixty seconds of history, because it explains every constraint in this act. From the CSI GA
announcement, Kubernetes 1.13, January 2019: volume plugins used to be in-tree, "meaning
their code was part of the core Kubernetes code and shipped with the core Kubernetes
binaries", so vendors "were forced to align with the Kubernetes release process". The blog is
blunt about why that had to change: third-party storage code "caused reliability and security
issues in core Kubernetes binaries".

So CSI is a divorce, and a good one. The vendor ships and versions their own driver, Kubernetes
stops carrying code it cannot test, and the storage layer becomes "truly extensible".

The bill arrives in the last bullet, and it is the thesis of the whole act: once the driver is
someone else's program, what your storage can do is whatever that program advertises. Snapshot,
expand, modify — each one optional. That is why a GA Kubernetes API can still be a no.

Do not go deeper than this. The next slide shows the calls themselves.

This is the slide that makes CSI make sense, so go slowly and read one row out loud:
"you write a PVC — the external-provisioner is watching for PVCs — it calls CreateVolume on

The spec defines three services: Identity, Controller and Node. The rows above are Controller
calls; the band below is Node calls.

Identity is how the last bullet of the previous slide actually works: `GetPluginCapabilities`
is literally the driver telling Kubernetes which of these calls it supports. Point back at it.

That is also why a CSI outage is a control-plane outage, not a data-plane one — the FAQ
slide later leans on exactly this.

Two halves worth naming: a Deployment (the controller side, the rows above) and a DaemonSet

## Your volume pins your pod

- One line on the **StorageClass** decides this: `volumeBindingMode`
- `Immediate` builds it now; `WaitForFirstConsumer` waits for the scheduler.
- The PV keeps that zone forever; when it fills or fails: `volume node affinity conflict`

<figure>
<svg class="d" viewBox="0 0 1014 148" role="img" aria-label="A zone is one availability zone; Immediate binding creates the disk before any pod is scheduled, WaitForFirstConsumer waits for the scheduler">

<!--
Land it: The storage layer quietly decides your availability domain

WHY THIS SLIDE IS HERE, in one sentence you can say out loud: the last two slides showed you
that provisioning is a call somebody makes — this one is about WHEN that call fires, because
that timing is what welds a database replica to one failure domain for the rest of its life.

The script, four beats:

1. "CreateVolume has to happen somewhere." A cloud disk is not cluster-wide. It is born in one
   zone, and it cannot leave. So the moment it is created, a zone has been chosen for every pod
   that will ever use it.
2. "volumeBindingMode decides who chooses." Immediate means the driver provisions as soon as
   the claim exists — before any pod, so before anyone knows where there is room, or which zone
   your other replicas are in. WaitForFirstConsumer means the claim sits Pending on purpose
   until the scheduler places the pod, and only then does the driver create the disk, in the
   right zone. This is why WaitForFirstConsumer is the default on every managed cluster's class.
3. "Then it is written down, permanently." The PV gets a nodeAffinity stanza naming that zone.
   The scheduler treats it as hard. Nothing rewrites it later.
4. "Which flips the mental model." People picture the volume following the pod around, like a
   process migrating. It is the exact opposite: the pod is dragged to wherever the disk already
   is, and if that place is full, or gone, the pod does not run.

The payoff line, and the reason this belongs in the act about Kubernetes rather than the act
about operators: nothing in your CR, your StatefulSet or your operator can undo this. The zone
was chosen by a driver, on the strength of one field on a StorageClass, possibly months ago.

The failure signature is on the slide because it is the thing people actually meet:
`volume node affinity conflict` in the pod's events. When you see it, stop reading the pod and
run `kubectl get pv <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeAffinity}'` — the answer is always a zone
that no longer has room for you.

Databases make this worse than stateless apps: three replicas, three zonal disks, and a
scheduler that must satisfy all three at once. Lose a zone and you do not lose a pod, you lose
a member that cannot be replaced until the zone returns — or until you delete the claim and
pay for a full clone, which is the act-three slide arriving as a bill.
-->

nothing in `kubectl get pods` hinting at it. One pod restart away from losing that replica's
data — pvc-protection was not protecting it, it was postponing it. Find yours with:

  kubectl get pvc -A -o json | jq -r '.items[]|select(.metadata.deletionTimestamp)|.metadata.name'

Triage commands worth saying out loud:
  kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
  kubectl describe pvc/<name> -n <ns>
  kubectl get volumeattachment

## They own the storage stack. We don't.

- Cloud DBaaS providers can reason about storage because they **own the whole storage stack**
- Kubernetes operators don't: not the disk, not the driver, not the node
- So how close can we get with the signals and control surfaces Kubernetes gives us?

<!--

## No single layer sees the whole I/O path

<figure>
<svg class="d" viewBox="0 0 948 306" role="img" aria-label="Seven layers between the engine and the disk, each able to queue, each invisible from the layer above">

  <rect class="box" x="0" y="62" width="700" height="34" rx="8"/>

  <rect class="box" x="0" y="100" width="700" height="34" rx="8"/>
  <text class="sm" x="20" y="117" dominant-baseline="middle">Linux page cache / filesystem</text>
  <rect class="box" x="0" y="138" width="700" height="34" rx="8"/>
  <text class="sm" x="20" y="155" dominant-baseline="middle">block layer and cgroup throttling</text>

  <text class="sm" x="20" y="231" dominant-baseline="middle">cloud block-storage service</text>
  <rect class="box" x="0" y="252" width="700" height="34" rx="8"/>

</svg>

## Ask the engine, ask the device

<figure>
<svg class="d" viewBox="0 0 948 244" role="img" aria-label="Engine-side and device-side latency for the same disk, measured on a live cluster">
  <rect class="box-a" x="0" y="20" width="462" height="150" rx="10"/>
  <text class="xs" x="20" y="44">ASK THE ENGINE</text>
  <text class="mono" x="20" y="70" dominant-baseline="middle" style="font-size:12px">performance_schema.file_summary_by_event_name</text>
  <text class="sm b" x="20" y="104" dominant-baseline="middle">dblwr write: avg 18.5 ms · max 408 ms</text>
  <text class="sm b" x="20" y="130" dominant-baseline="middle">log fsync: avg 4.5 ms · max 273 ms</text>
  <text class="xs" x="20" y="158">what the database experienced</text>
  <rect class="box-a" x="486" y="20" width="462" height="150" rx="10"/>
  <text class="xs" x="506" y="44">ASK THE DEVICE</text>
  <text class="mono" x="506" y="70" dominant-baseline="middle" style="font-size:12px">grep sdb /proc/diskstats · inside the pod</text>
  <text class="sm b" x="506" y="104" dominant-baseline="middle">11,774 writes / 70,861 ms = 6.0 ms</text>
  <text class="xs" x="506" y="158">what the kernel measured</text>
  <rect class="box" x="0" y="188" width="948" height="56" rx="10" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
  <text class="sm b" x="20" y="212" dominant-baseline="middle">the engine waits longer than the device reports</text>
  <text class="xs" x="20" y="234" dominant-baseline="middle">that gap is queueing and fsync, not the disk being slow. one number alone would have blamed the wrong layer.</text>
</svg>
</figure>

<!--
Land it: Two numbers for the same disk, and they disagree on purpose

Both of these are from ps-cluster1 on my own GKE cluster, taken while writing this talk, on a
cluster doing almost nothing. Say that: these are idle numbers, and they are still interesting.

The engine number is a wait: how long InnoDB sat there. The device number is service time: how
long the kernel's request took. When the first is much larger than the second, you are queued
or you are paying for fsync, and no amount of faster disk fixes it.

Both commands work on any cluster, today, with no exporters installed. That is the point of
this pair — it is the floor of what you can see, not the ceiling.
-->

## Ask Kubernetes, ask the cloud

<figure>
<svg class="d" viewBox="0 0 948 250" role="img" aria-label="What Kubernetes and the cloud provider will each tell you about the same volume">

  <text class="xs" x="20" y="44">ASK KUBERNETES</text>
  <text class="mono" x="20" y="70" dominant-baseline="middle" style="font-size:12px">nodes/&lt;node&gt;/proxy/metrics</text>
  <text class="sm b" x="20" y="102" dominant-baseline="middle">kubelet_volume_stats_*: 207 MiB of 1.9 GiB</text>
  <text class="sm" x="20" y="128" dominant-baseline="middle">cAdvisor: per-pod blkio, per device</text>
  <text class="xs" x="20" y="160">capacity and attribution. no latency.</text>
  <rect class="box-a" x="486" y="20" width="462" height="156" rx="10"/>
  <text class="xs" x="506" y="44">ASK THE CLOUD</text>

  <text class="sm b" x="506" y="102" dominant-baseline="middle">pd-balanced, 2 GB, no provisioned IOPS</text>

<!--
Land it: Kubernetes tells you how full it is. Only the provider tells you how fast it is.

This is the asymmetry from the top of the act, made concrete. kubelet_volume_stats gives you
capacity and nothing else — no IOPS, no latency, no queue. The numbers that decide whether
storage is your problem are in the provider's monitoring API, one identity boundary away.

The band matters and it is measured, not assumed: I looked for the CSI controller on my GKE
cluster and it is not there. Only `pdcsi-node`, the DaemonSet, runs in kube-system. So the
sidecar metrics people tell you to scrape do not exist on a managed cluster.

Two GCP metrics worth naming: `performance_status`, a Healthy/Degraded boolean per disk, and

engine was reporting milliseconds. Different layers, different truths, both real.

## The one knob Kubernetes gives you, refused 💥

```yaml
kind: VolumeAttributesClass          # storage.k8s.io/v1, GA
driverName: pd.csi.storage.gke.io
parameters: { iops: "3000", throughput: "150" }
```

- Patch it onto a bound claim and the driver answers, in its own words:

```console
VolumeModifyFailed  rpc error: code = InvalidArgument desc =
  Failed to modify volume: modifications not supported for disk type pd-balanced
```

<!--
Land it: A GA API, a working driver, and a flat no — because the disk underneath has no such knob

Measured on the same cluster, minutes before this talk was finalised. The PVC status goes to
`{"status":"Infeasible","targetVolumeAttributesClassName":"probe-iops"}` and stays there.

Worth admitting on stage: my first attempt failed for a different reason, wrong parameter
names, and that error looked identical from the outside — Infeasible. I nearly reported it as
proof. The second run is the real refusal, and it names the disk type explicitly.

This is the whole talk in one event message. The API layer is GA. The driver implements
ControllerModifyVolume. And pd-balanced still has nothing to modify, so your one control
surface returns InvalidArgument. To change it you change the disk type, which means a new
class, a new volume and a restore.
-->

<!-- _class: dark -->

## The metrics that can mislead you

- `iostat %util` at 100% means the device was **busy**, not that it was saturated
- An average stays calm through the tail latency your users actually felt
- The node looks healthy while one cgroup is throttled to a crawl
- Free space looks fine while size-derived performance is the real limit

<!--
Land it: Every one of these has ended a debugging session early, and wrongly

On %util, because someone always asks where the number comes from: it is the iostat column,
fed by io_ticks in /proc/diskstats, and it means "at least one request was in flight" for that
share of wall-clock time. It was a good saturation signal for one spinning disk that served
one request at a time. A cloud volume serves many in parallel, so 100% only means never idle —
you can sit there at a tenth of the device's capability. Queue depth and latency are the
signals that actually say saturated.

The contrarian slide. Expect one argument in Q&A, and welcome it — the %util one is the
argument you'll get, and you're right, but be gracious about it.
-->

<!-- _class: dark -->

## What the operator can actually do

- Grow the volume before it fills, and record `currentSize`, `resizeCount`, `lastError` in status
- Surface storage failures as events on the CR, not buried in kubelet logs
- Ensure per-pod storage signals are collected before the incident
- Run backups from a replica, so durability stops competing with production reads
- Name the driver's refusal, `StorageClassNotSupportResize`, instead of retrying blindly

<!--
Land it: The operator's real job here is to make the storage layer legible

This is the answer to "so what should my operator do?" — reporting, not heroics. Nothing on
this list is clever; all of it is the difference between a 20-minute and a 3-hour incident.
-->

---

## What no operator can do for you

<figure>
<svg class="d" viewBox="0 0 1014 208" role="img" aria-label="Four things no operator can do, because they were decided at provisioning time">
  <rect class="box" x="0" y="20" width="494" height="72" rx="10" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
  <text class="sm b" x="22" y="48" dominant-baseline="middle">exceed what the backend offers</text>
  <text class="xs" x="22" y="74" dominant-baseline="middle">a VolumeAttributesClass can retune it, if the disk type allows</text>
  <rect class="box" x="520" y="20" width="494" height="72" rx="10" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
  <text class="sm b" x="542" y="48" dominant-baseline="middle">change a bound PVC's StorageClass</text>
  <text class="xs" x="542" y="74" dominant-baseline="middle">that is a migration, and always was</text>
  <rect class="box" x="0" y="106" width="494" height="72" rx="10" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
  <text class="sm b" x="22" y="134" dominant-baseline="middle">make cross-AZ latency smaller</text>
  <text class="xs" x="22" y="160" dominant-baseline="middle">than the distance</text>
  <rect class="box" x="520" y="106" width="494" height="72" rx="10" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
  <text class="sm b" x="542" y="134" dominant-baseline="middle">fix a snapshot after you took it</text>
  <text class="xs" x="542" y="160" dominant-baseline="middle">crash-consistent cannot become application-consistent later</text>
</svg>
</figure>

<!--
Land it: These are decisions that were already made, at provisioning time or at snapshot time

On the snapshot box, if anyone asks: a CSI VolumeSnapshot is crash-consistent by default, a
block-level copy as if the power went out. InnoDB will usually replay redo and come up, but
"usually" is not a backup strategy, and the copy is not atomic across two volumes if redo and
data are separate. Application-consistent means something flushed and quiesced the database
first, and there is no hook in the CSI spec that does that for you. An operator CAN coordinate
it at snapshot time, with a clone or XtraBackup. Nothing can add it afterwards.

Callback to Act two. The room should feel "Some PVC fields cannot change that easily" land retroactively —
that's the whole reason that slide is early.
-->

## Ideas to try

- **`kubectl get sc -o wide`**: provisioner, binding mode, expansion, in one line
  - three of the six failure modes were decided here, long before the incident
- **`kubectl -n kube-system get ds,deploy | grep csi`**: find your driver's pods
  - when a volume hangs, this is how you know whose logs to read and whose ticket to open
- **Ask MySQL how long a write took, then ask the disk**
  - MySQL waited 18 ms, the disk took 6. The other 12 never touched the disk
- **Point a `VolumeAttributesClass` at a claim you don't care about**
  - either it retunes the disk, or you learn today that your disk type has no knob

Every line is something I did on a live cluster while building this talk, which is the claim

 - the storage class check is one command and answers three of the six failure modes from
   act one, before anything is on fire.
 - the driver-pods one solves a real incident problem. A stuck claim is either a controller
   problem (provisioning, attaching) or a node problem (staging, mounting), and the logs live
   in different places. On GKE only pdcsi-node is in kube-system: the controller runs in the
   managed control plane, so there is no provisioner log for you to read and a stuck
   CreateVolume is a support ticket, not a kubectl session. On a self-managed cluster both
   halves are yours and both logs are readable. Two minutes now saves that discovery later.

   on a 1Gi claim beats any number you remember from a blog post.

   it waited; /proc/diskstats reports how long the device was busy. The difference is time the
   write spent queued, or waiting for fsync to make it durable. A faster disk only moves the
   smaller of the two numbers, which is why one measurement sends people to the wrong layer.
 - the kubelet/provider split is the asymmetry this act opened with: you cannot get IOPS or
   throttling from inside the cluster.
